claims.text: The starting material has a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
The lamellar phases are FCC plus B2, or FCC/L12 plus B2.
Internal lamellar boundaries in the untreated alloy promote dislocation pile-ups.
Dislocation pile-ups at the internal boundaries produce local stress concentrations.
The boundary-associated pile-ups and stress concentrations cause premature microcracking, limited ductility, and brittle or catastrophic failure.
A nanoscale ultrathin interlayer can be deposited selectively at lamellar colony interfaces, or equivalent interface-confined solute segregation can be induced in a single treatment.
The treatment will create chemically tailored, compositionally graded regions along the lamellar boundaries.
The tailored interlayer will facilitate smoother dislocation transmission across the dual-phase interfaces.
Smoother dislocation transmission will reduce dislocation pile-ups and local interfacial stress concentrations.
Reducing pile-ups and interfacial stress concentrations will delay microcrack initiation during tensile deformation.
The interfacial treatment will increase room-temperature uniform tensile elongation by approximately 10% or more relative to the untreated alloy.
The interfacial treatment will retain or slightly increase both yield strength and ultimate tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
Hierarchical microstructural engineering can simultaneously enhance strength and ductility in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
Nanoscale L12 precipitation in a lamellar FCC+B2 eutectic high-entropy alloy can substantially increase yield strength with only a small loss of elongation.
The proposed effect is applicable under room-temperature, quasi-static tensile loading.
The magnitude of improvement and the strength-ductility balance depend on interlayer chemistry, thickness, and uniformity.
